# How to Summarise a Long Article or PDF into Key Bullet Points

> **In short:** Paste the text (or upload the PDF) into any AI assistant, then use a short "summarise into bullet points" prompt. You'll get the main argument and the key takeaways in under five minutes — works in ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Copilot, Le Chat or DeepSeek.

You've just opened a 20-page report, a long news feature, or a 40-page PDF someone sent you. You don't have time to read all of it, but you do need to know what it actually says. This guide walks you through a simple workflow that turns a long document into a tight set of bullet points you can scan in a minute, using a prompt you can reuse on any AI assistant.

## Before you start
- **An AI assistant** you can type into — ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Copilot, Le Chat or DeepSeek all work. Pick the one you already have an account with.
- **A free plan is fine** for short articles. Uploading large PDFs (say, over 50 pages) may need a paid plan or a paid tier with bigger file limits — check the assistant's current limits if your file is very long.
- **The article or PDF you want summarised.** Have it open in another tab, or saved on your device.
- **Roughly 5 minutes** from opening the assistant to having your bullet-point summary ready.

One honest note before you start: an AI summary is a starting point, not a replacement for reading. If the document is something important (a contract, a medical paper, a policy that affects you), treat the summary as a map of the territory, not the territory itself. Use it to decide what to read carefully.

## Step 1 — Open your AI assistant and find the chat box
Open the website or app of your chosen AI assistant in a browser, or launch the mobile app. Look for the chat box — the long text field at the bottom of the screen, usually with a placeholder line like *"Message [assistant name]…"* or *"Ask anything…"*. Tap or click inside it so your cursor is blinking in the field. If you're on a phone and don't see a text field, look for a round **+** or **new chat** button on the home screen, then start a fresh conversation. A new, blank chat is ideal — older messages in the thread can confuse the summary, and the assistant only has a limited "memory" of what you paste in (this is called the **context window** — think of it as the assistant's short-term working memory, the amount of text it can actively read in one go).
💬 Example: type nothing yet — just confirm the chat is open and ready.
You'll know it worked when you see an empty text field with a send button (usually a paper-plane icon or an up-arrow) next to it.

## Step 2 — Get the text you want summarised ready
Open the article or PDF in another window. You have two options, and which one is easier depends on the assistant and the file type. **Option A (easiest for articles):** select the text in the article, copy it (Ctrl+C on Windows, Cmd+C on Mac, or long-press and "Copy" on a phone), then switch back to the chat. **Option B (easiest for PDFs):** look for a **paperclip icon** 📎, an **attachment icon**, or a **+** button near the chat box — many assistants let you upload a PDF directly. If you don't see a paperclip, look for a menu labelled "Add files", "Upload" or similar. If neither option works, fall back to opening the PDF in a reader, selecting the text, copying it, and pasting it into the chat as plain text.
💬 Example: highlight the first few paragraphs of a long article, copy them, and have your clipboard ready.
You'll know it worked when you either have text highlighted and copied, or a file ready to upload in the chat.

## Step 3 — Paste the text or upload the PDF
Click into the chat box and paste the text (Ctrl+V / Cmd+V, or long-press and "Paste" on a phone). The text will appear inside the chat field as a block of words. If you're uploading a PDF, tap the paperclip or **+** button, choose your file from the list, and wait for the upload progress bar to finish — a small file thumbnail or filename usually appears in the chat field once it's uploaded. If the assistant says the file is "too large", try copying just the first half of the text and pasting it as plain text instead. On the free plan, file size limits are common, and they change often.
💬 Example: paste a 3,000-word article into the chat, or upload a 12-page PDF called *"Q3-strategy-review.pdf"*.
You'll know it worked when you can see the pasted text block (or the uploaded file name) sitting in the chat field, ready to send.

## Step 4 — Add a "summarise into bullet points" prompt
This is the most important step. The quality of your summary depends almost entirely on the instruction you give the assistant. A vague request like "summarise this" usually gives you a waffly paragraph. A specific request gives you clean, scannable bullets. Type the following prompt directly under the pasted text or uploaded file, then send the message (press the paper-plane or up-arrow button). The assistant will start "reading" the content, and within a few seconds you'll see bullet points appear.
💬 Example: *"Please summarise this into bullet points. I want: 1) the main argument or thesis in one sentence, 2) the 5–7 key takeaways as short bullets, 3) any important numbers, dates or names mentioned, 4) one sentence on what the author is asking the reader to do or believe. Keep it under 250 words."*
You'll know it worked when the assistant replies with a structured list of bullets (not a long paragraph), and you can identify the main point within the first three bullets.

## Step 5 — Check the summary and ask for a tweak
Read the bullet points. Ask yourself: do I now know what this document is actually about? If the summary is too long, too vague, or missing the main point, send a short follow-up. The assistant remembers the original document in the same chat, so you can refine without re-pasting anything. If the summary missed something, name what you wanted. If it's too long, ask for it shorter. If you want a different angle — say, the parts that affect your job — ask for that view.
💬 Example: *"That's good. Now give me just the 3 bullets most relevant to a small business owner."* or *"Cut this down to 5 bullets maximum."*
You'll know it worked when the second reply gives you a summary that you can read in under a minute and confidently explain to someone else.

## Step 6 — Save or share the result
Once you're happy with the summary, copy it out of the chat (select the assistant's reply, copy, and paste into a note, email or document). If your assistant has a **share** or **copy** button near the reply, use that — it's usually faster. Saving the bullets somewhere means you don't have to come back to the chat later, and you can paste them into a meeting agenda, a study note, or a message to a colleague. Over time, building a small folder of "bullet summaries" is a quiet superpower for keeping up with reading you don't have time to do properly.
💬 Example: paste the bullets into a note called *"Reading — June 2026"*, with a one-line note above them saying where they came from.
You'll know it worked when the summary is saved in a place you can find again, and you can skim it in under a minute the next time you need it.

## Common mistakes
- **Asking a vague question.** "Summarise this" usually gets you a wobbly paragraph. Always specify the format: bullet points, a number of bullets, and what you want covered (main argument, key takeaways, numbers). The more specific the instruction, the better the output.
- **Pasting a 50-page PDF as plain text.** If the document is very long and you paste it all in, the assistant may quietly drop the middle of the text because of the context window limit. For long files, use the PDF upload option if your assistant offers one, or paste just the introduction and the conclusion first to get a quick orientation.
- **Trusting the summary without a sanity check.** AI assistants sometimes invent a number, a name, or a quote that isn't in the original. If a bullet contains a specific fact that matters to you, scroll back to the original document and confirm it's there. Treat surprising claims as a prompt to verify, not as confirmed truth.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** Got a long newsletter, a council report, or a terms-of-service update you don't want to read in full? Run it through this workflow in five minutes and you'll know whether it's worth your time.
- **For your business or work:** Use it on meeting prep notes, industry reports, competitor blog posts, or long client briefs. A bullet summary you can re-read in 60 seconds is far more useful than a document you read once and never open again.
- **If you're just getting started:** Pick one document you've been meaning to read — an article someone sent you, a report you bookmarked — and run it through Steps 1–6 today. The first time feels slow; the second time is genuinely five minutes.

## Try it now
Open the assistant you use most, find a long article you've been putting off, and run it through this exact prompt: *"Please summarise this into bullet points. I want: 1) the main argument in one sentence, 2) the 5–7 key takeaways as short bullets, 3) any important numbers or dates, 4) one sentence on what the author wants the reader to do or believe. Keep it under 250 words."* Five minutes, one document, one useful habit started.
